foodDescription: Round dumplings of grated raw and boiled potato, often stuffed with minced meat, served under fried onion and pork crackling. A Praga dish: women once sold them hot from jars at Bazar Różyckiego, the old east-bank market. Heavy, so plan a walk after.

Pork loin beaten thin, breaded and fried in lard until the edges curl, served with boiled potatoes and dill and a side of cabbage or cucumber salad. The Polish Sunday lunch. Milk bars do a cheap and honest one; the plate rarely leaves room for dessert.

Thin beef slices rolled around pickled cucumber, bacon and onion, tied with string and braised soft in dark gravy. Served with buckwheat groats or mashed potato. Old-school Warsaw restaurants keep them on the menu. Check for the string before you bite.

Cabbage leaves wrapped around minced pork and rice, baked or simmered and served under tomato or mushroom sauce. The name means little pigeons, and nobody can say why. A milk-bar staple and a home-cooking test: the leaf should cut with a fork.

Tomato soup made on the stock left from Sunday’s chicken broth, with rice or thin noodles and a swirl of sour cream. The Monday soup of every Polish household and every milk bar. Sweeter and creamier than a Spanish or Italian version, and cheap everywhere.

A cold summer soup of young beetroot and its leaves stirred into kefir or soured milk with cucumber, radish and dill, usually topped with half a boiled egg. Shocking pink and sharp. Only on menus in hot months, so order it when you see it.

Grated potato and onion fried in thin, crisp-edged pancakes. Eaten with sour cream or sugar, or folded around goulash as placek po węgiersku, Hungarian-style. A milk-bar classic; the ones fried to order beat the ones sitting under the lamp.

Thin pancakes folded around sweetened curd cheese, jam or fruit, sometimes fried again in butter and topped with cream. A cheap lunch rather than a dessert in milk bars like Prasowy on Marszałkowska Street. Savoury versions come with spinach or mushrooms.

Salted herring in oil with raw onion, or in sour cream with apple, eaten as a zakąska, a bite between shots of vodka. Warsaw’s late-night bars serve it for a few złoty a plate, the Polish currency. One shot, one bite is the rhythm.

Raw chopped beef with a raw egg yolk on top, surrounded by diced pickles, onion and pickled mushrooms that you mix in yourself. A starter in old restaurants and a vodka snack in all-night bars. The yolk may come in its half-shell so you can add it slowly.

Chocolate sponge soaked in punch, layered with thick whipped cream and covered in chocolate glaze. Created in Warsaw around 1950, most likely named after the W-Z route, the postwar east–west road through the rebuilt centre. Eat it with a fork, carefully.

Squares of soft vanilla mousse coated in chocolate, invented by Warsaw chocolatier Jan Wedel in 1936. The name is from the saying that a rich man has everything but bird’s milk. Sold in every corner shop; the vanilla box is the original.

Melted chocolate rather than cocoa, thick enough to stand a spoon in, served in Wedel’s chocolate lounges, the oldest on Szpitalna Street in the city centre. Order it plain or with chilli and expect to finish with a spoon. A glass of water helps.

A pink-and-white chewy sugar sweet, made in Praga since the 19th century. Sold from stalls outside Warsaw cemeteries such as Powązki on All Saints’ Day, 1 November. It sticks to your teeth; that is the point.

Fruit simmered in water with a little sugar and served cold in a glass, often with the fruit still in it: strawberries in summer, apples and plums in autumn. The default drink with a milk-bar lunch. Home versions vary wildly in sweetness.
